opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions right now, but I'd frame it carefully.

The appeal is obvious. A lot of classic interpretability is very manual: you find a neuron or a direction, stare at examples, run some interventions, and write up a story. That doesn't scale to models with billions of parameters and millions of features. So the idea of training a model, often a language model, to read another model's activations and tell you in plain language what's going on is really attractive. You're using the same scaling that made these systems so capable to help us understand them.

What I care about most, coming from a causal perspective, is whether the explanation is actually *faithful*. It's very easy to train an explainer that produces plausible-sounding descriptions. Language models are great at sounding plausible. But does the explanation track what the underlying model is really computing? If the explainer says "this representation encodes that the user is upset," then intervening on that representation in the way the explanation predicts should change the model's behavior accordingly. If it doesn't, you've built a very fluent storyteller, not an interpretability tool.

So my assessment is: promising, with a big asterisk on evaluation. The approaches I find most convincing ground the training signal in something causal or verifiable rather than just matching human-written labels. You could train the explainer to predict what happens under interventions, or to answer questions whose answers you can check against the model's actual behavior.

There's also a nice recursive worry: now you have to interpret the interpreter. I don't think that's fatal. In practice, if the explainer's outputs are checkable, you don't need to fully understand its internals, just as we trust a calculator without inspecting its circuits. But it means benchmarks and rigorous baselines matter a lot. In some of our own work we've seen that fancy interpretability methods sometimes don't beat simple baselines like prompting or linear probes on practical tasks like steering or concept detection. Any new paradigm, including trained explainers, should be held to that standard.

So I'm optimistic. I think this kind of scalable, learned interpretability is probably where the field is heading. But the real progress will come from people who are obsessive about measuring whether the explanations are true, not just whether they read well.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss sparse autoencoders or whether their objective captures researchers’ interpretability goals.

r003.rationale: It describes reading activations and explaining them in plain language, but not reconstructing representations through a natural-language bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It questions whether plausible-sounding explanations faithfully track the model’s computation and proposes checking them through interventions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the more promising directions in interpretability right now, but I want to be careful about what it is and isn't buying us.

The basic idea is that instead of a human sitting with a sparse autoencoder feature or an attention head and trying to write a label by hand, you train a model, often a fairly capable one, to look at activations or circuits of a target model and produce explanations, or predict behavior, or answer questions about what the target is doing. The appeal is obvious. The target model has billions of parameters and the number of interesting internal objects is enormous. Humans don't scale. A model that can read activations and tell you what they mean, at least approximately, is the only thing that plausibly scales to frontier-sized systems.

Where I get cautious is on two fronts. The first is validation. If a model tells you "this direction encodes whether the user is asking about medical topics," how do you know that's true? The honest answer is you need a behavioral check, an intervention, a steering experiment, something causal. Otherwise you've just moved the problem from "I don't understand the model" to "I don't understand the explainer, and I'm trusting its story." The best work in this space treats the explainer as a hypothesis generator and then grades those hypotheses against actual interventions on the target. If you skip that step, you can get very fluent, very plausible explanations that are just wrong, and fluent-but-wrong is arguably worse than nothing.

The second concern is the alignment of incentives between the two models. If you train the interpreter to produce explanations humans rate highly, you're optimizing for explanations that sound good to humans, which is not the same thing as explanations that are faithful. And there's a subtler version of this: if the interpreter and the target share training data or architecture, they may share blind spots. The interpreter may find it natural to describe the target's internals in terms that are convenient for a language model, not in terms that reflect what's actually happening computationally.

That said, I don't want to be too negative. The things I find genuinely exciting are the cases where you can set up the task so the interpreter is scored on something objective, like predicting the target's outputs on held-out inputs from the internal state, or predicting the effect of an ablation before you run it. Those are tasks where you can't fake it. The interpreter either understands the representation well enough to make the prediction or it doesn't. If we can build a pipeline where the interpreter is constantly being checked against ground truth like that, then I think training a model to interpret another model goes from a nice demo to something you could actually rely on in an audit.

So my assessment is: necessary in the long run, because nothing else scales, but only as good as the grounding you attach to it. The interesting research question isn't "can a model explain another model," it's "how do we make the explanations falsifiable."

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising approach, but we need to distinguish generating an explanation from verifying that explanation. A large model might look at examples where a neuron or a feature activates and give you a very plausible description of what it represents. That’s useful—it can help us explore far more of a network than we could manually. But a plausible description isn’t necessarily an accurate account of what the network is doing.

The next step should be to turn that description into a testable prediction. Does it predict when the feature will activate on new inputs? And if we intervene on that feature, does the model’s behavior change in the way the explanation suggests? Those tests give us stronger evidence than simply asking another model whether the explanation sounds right.

So I’d treat the interpreting model as a tool for generating hypotheses. The fact that it’s also a complex model doesn’t make it useless, but it means we shouldn’t take its explanations on trust. The value comes from connecting those explanations to experiments we can independently check.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising approach, but we have to be precise about what we mean by “interpretable.” A large model can look at examples that activate a neuron or a feature and produce a very plausible explanation. That can help us explore representations much faster. But a plausible explanation isn’t necessarily a faithful account of what the model is doing.

The key is to make those explanations testable. If we say a feature represents a particular concept, can we predict when it will activate on new examples? And if we intervene on that feature, does the model’s behavior change in the way our explanation predicts? Those are stronger checks than simply asking whether the explanation sounds reasonable.

There’s also a risk that we’ve moved the problem one level up: now we’re relying on another model whose reasoning we don’t fully understand. That doesn’t make the approach useless. It means I’d treat the explaining model as a tool for generating hypotheses, with experiments providing the evidence. The exciting possibility is using models to scale up that whole process—proposing explanations, designing tests, and finding where the explanations break.
